newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Israel orders Bezeq workers back on line.
newsitem.headline: Israel orders Bezeq workers back on line.

text.p: The Israeli government issued an order on Wednesday to force hundreds of Bezeq Israel Telecom employees to restore essential telephone services after strikers refused to comply fully with a back-to-work court order.

Union leaders at Israel's main telecoms provider called the move "totalitarian" and said a crisis continued over government plans to privatise more of the state-owned company through the $250 million sale of 12.5 percent of its stock to Merrill Lynch.

"The government...decided today to enact emergency regulations so we can in effect issue a restraining order against some 440 workers in essential Bezeq services," Communications Minister Limor Livnat told Israel Radio.
"We decided on this order after the workers breached yesterday's labour court order," she said. "This step is not being taken with great joy but only because there is no choice."

The week-long Bezeq strike has left thousands of homes and businesses without full telephone services and forced the Tel Aviv Stock Exchange to halt trading on Tuesday. Disruptions continued on Wednesday but the bourse reopened for business.
Striking Bezeq workers returned to their workplaces on Wednesday, saying they had complied with the Tel Aviv labour court order, but did not restore normal telephone services.

"Employees returned to their workplaces but how can you expect them to work as usual, under a court order, when they are troubled and have no assurances of their future?" Bezeq union spokesman Tzvi Vilnai said.
Vilnai called Livnat's move to force workers back to their jobs "ridiculous". "If she wants to manage things in a totalitarian fashion she will get a response in kind," he said.
Livnat said the order was intended to ensure communications for hospitals, police and emergency services.

The labour court on Wednesday rejected a request by Bezeq management to find workers in contempt of court but again ordered them to restore services and open negotiations with the Government Corporations Authority, which oversees privatisation, and the Communications Ministry.
The Merrill Lynch deal which sparked the strike involves 90.6 million shares, or 12.5 percent of Bezeq stock. Bezeq is 76 percent government-owned.
The first tranche of 2.5 percent of shares is being sold for $50 million, or five percent below the market value on July 10. Merrill Lynch cannot return these shares to the government.

An additional 10 percent is being sold at market value for $200 million. Merrill Lynch has five months from September 1 to sell these shares to its clients. The government has agreed to buy back any stock from this package that remains unsold.

Union leaders said the deal violated government promises to involve Bezeq workers in all aspects of the company's privatisation and called for the sale to be cancelled or to use its revenues to fund early pension programmes.
"The crisis is far from over," Vilnai said. "Workers are still demanding the cancellation of the Merrill Lynch deal."
Union leaders of government firms threatened to shut down air and sea ports, trains, postal services, Israel's electric company, and health funds in solidarity with the Bezeq workers.

"Every privatisation must be put to the workers...If there is no agreement we may find ourselves in a position where we need to act," Shlomo Shani, trade union department chief of the Histadrut labour federation, told Reuters.
Union leaders were due to meet Wednesday night to decide whether to go on strike on Thursday.
